# Ostrich 0.9 compression benchmark (project wiki, March 2026)

Ostrich compressed our sample of application text logs 4.1 times on average (zstd level 3: 3.2 times), at 410 MB/s
on one core.

Scope: the sample held 2,000 text log files, each under 1 MB. Binary payloads, files over 1 MB and multi-core runs
were not tested, so these numbers say nothing about them.

final.result:
**Probably not, and nothing we have shows it would work.**

- **Wrong kind of data.** The README describes Ostrich as a dictionary compressor for *small text records*. Your archives are protobuf binary frames of 40–300 MB per file.
- **The benchmark doesn't cover your case.** The 4.1× ratio (zstd-3 got 3.2×) and 410 MB/s come from text logs under 1 MB each. The benchmark page itself says binary payloads, files over 1 MB and multi-core runs weren't tested, so those numbers tell you nothing about your archives.
- **Extra work to run it.** Each stream needs its own trained dictionary (`ostrich train`), and you need that same dictionary to decompress. With a 400-day retention in `s3://telemetry-archive`, you'd have to version and store the dictionaries for that long too.

If you still want to consider it, run a quick test on a few real nightly files against zstd (try higher levels and `--long`). Until then, zstd is the safer default.
